body:
Exchange in an economy without widespread coinage

Vedic communities produced different goods: livestock and animal products, agricultural produce, pottery, textiles and tools. Since households did not necessarily produce everything they needed, they could obtain goods through exchange.

Barter is the direct exchange of one good or service for another without using money as the medium of payment. For example, a cultivator might exchange grain for a pot or a useful tool. This example illustrates how barter works; it does not establish a fixed exchange rate used throughout the Vedic Period.

Barter was important in the Vedic economy, but it was not the only way valuable goods changed hands. Gifts, the transfer of wealth after conflict and exchanges involving valued objects also formed part of economic life.

Gifts and the distribution of wealth

In the early Vedic setting, cattle and other goods were important forms of wealth. A leader could receive valuable goods, while priests and other community members could receive a share of wealth or gifts.

Dana refers to a gift or donation. A gift differs from an ordinary market exchange because the recipient does not necessarily provide an agreed good of equal value in return. Gifts could express support, honour or social relationships.

Some goods obtained during warfare were also distributed. These transfers were not identical to the regular compulsory taxes of later territorial kingdoms.

Valued metals and the meaning of nishka

Gold and other valuable materials were known in Vedic society. The term nishka occurs in discussions of Vedic wealth and exchange. In early contexts, it is often understood as a gold ornament or valued piece of gold.

A reference to a valuable gold object does not necessarily prove the existence of a standardised, officially minted coin. Punch-marked coins became important in the early historic economy, associated with growing trade and states from around the 6th century BCE onward.

Valuable object and coin are not the same

A gold ornament can hold value and be exchanged without being a standardised minted coin. Do not treat every Vedic reference to gold or nishka as evidence of a developed coinage system.

From gifts to regular taxation

As territorial kingdoms developed, rulers increasingly required dependable resources to maintain officials, soldiers and fortified settlements. Occasional gifts alone could not meet every recurring expense.

By the age of the mahajanapadas, from about the 6th century BCE, rulers collected regular taxes and other dues. Agriculture was especially important because cultivators produced much of the food and a significant share of the resources available to the state.

One important tax was bhaga, meaning the ruler's share of agricultural produce. Textbook accounts commonly describe this as usually 1/6 of the crop in the mahajanapada setting. This should not be interpreted as a uniform tax rate that applied to every Vedic community in every period.

Other demands could fall on craftspeople, herders and traders. Craftspeople might provide labour, herders could give animals or animal products, and goods involved in trade could be taxed.

Three different economic transfers

It is useful to distinguish the purpose of a transfer rather than identifying it only by the object transferred.

  • Exchange or barter: Goods are transferred to obtain other goods or services.
  • Gift: Goods are presented without the same direct exchange requirement.
  • Tax: A ruler or state claims a required contribution under its authority.

The same material, such as grain or livestock, could be involved in different kinds of transfer. What distinguishes them is the relationship between the giver and the recipient.

Prelims focus

  • Barter means direct exchange without money as the payment medium.
  • Dana means gift or donation.
  • Nishka in an early Vedic context does not by itself prove the use of standardised minted coins.
  • Punch-marked coins belong to the growing early historic monetary economy.
  • Bhaga was a share of agricultural produce, commonly described as usually 1/6 in the mahajanapada setting.
  • Trap: Gifts and regular taxation were different mechanisms of obtaining resources.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, 2018–19 edition, Chapter 5, printed pp. 46–47, Chapter 6, printed pp. 58–60, and Chapter 9, printed pp. 90–92; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 2, 'Kings, Farmers and Towns', section 2.1, printed pp. 29–30; INFLIBNET e-PG Pathshala, Outlines of Indian History, 'Vedic Culture', sections 5.4 and 6.3 (consulted 17 November 2026).]

pictures.alt: Barter exchanges goods without money; gifts require no equivalent return; taxes are compulsory. Bhaga was usually 1/6 of the crop.
pictures.caption: Barter, gifts and taxation involved different economic relationships.

title: Exchange, Wealth, Gifts and the Rise of Regular Revenue

body:
Changing patterns of settlement

Between the Early Vedic Period and the emergence of the mahajanapadas, many communities in northern India experienced changes in their livelihoods and settlements. Cattle rearing remained important, while more extensive cultivation supported increasingly settled populations in suitable regions.

The change was gradual and uneven. Some communities continued to rely heavily on livestock or other activities, and not every agricultural village developed into a town.

From jana to janapada

The word jana referred to a people or community. Janapada literally refers to the land where a jana sets its foot or settles. The term therefore reflects the growing importance of an identifiable territory associated with a community.

In the later Vedic setting, territories associated with communities such as the Kurus and Panchalas became significant in the upper Ganga-Yamuna region. Settlements were linked by cultivation, livestock keeping, crafts and exchange.

Archaeological sites associated with janapada settlements include Purana Qila in Delhi, Hastinapura near Meerut and Atranjikhera near Etah. At these sites, evidence includes domestic settlements, livestock, crops and pottery such as Painted Grey Ware.

Why agricultural settlements could grow

Several economic developments helped support larger and more lasting settlements.

  • Greater cultivation: More productive farming in suitable areas increased the quantity of food available.
  • Animal power: Oxen helped with cultivation and transport.
  • Iron tools: In some environments, stronger cutting tools and ploughshares supported agricultural and other work.
  • Water management: Access to rivers and appropriate irrigation facilities made cultivation more dependable in certain areas.
  • Craft production and exchange: Goods could move between cultivators, herders, artisans and other people.

Where food production exceeded immediate household consumption, part of the output could support people who did not cultivate their own food. This was one of the conditions that made larger settlements and more varied occupations possible.

These developments did not operate independently. Agricultural production needed labour and tools, while artisans and other specialists depended on food and access to materials.

Mahajanapadas and the growth of towns

From around the 6th century BCE, some janapadas grew into larger and more powerful territorial states called mahajanapadas. Many developed fortified capitals and increasingly organised systems for collecting resources.

Fortified settlements, armies and officials required a dependable economic base. Agricultural taxes, dues on crafts and trade, and other resources helped support these activities.

Early towns also served as places of production, exchange, administration and movement along routes connecting different regions. Their growth formed part of a wider change often called the second urbanisation of ancient India.

First urbanisation and second urbanisation

The term second urbanisation distinguishes the growth of early historic towns, particularly from around the 6th century BCE, from the much earlier urban centres of the Harappan Civilisation.

For a Gujarat connection, Dholavira and Lothal were important Harappan centres of the earlier Bronze Age civilisation. They should not be treated as examples of towns that first arose because of later Vedic iron technology. The Mature Harappan urban phase is conventionally dated to about 2600–1900 BCE, substantially earlier than the mahajanapadas.

Agricultural growth did not have a single cause

The growth of settlements and early states was linked to changes in cultivation, tools, water use, crafts, exchange and political organisation. It is inaccurate to explain the entire process as the automatic result of the introduction of iron.

The broad economic sequence

For prelims preparation, the most useful chronological distinction is between an early Vedic economy in which cattle were especially prominent, a later Vedic setting in which settled cultivation became more important in many northern regions, and the expanding early historic economy of fortified capitals, regular taxation, greater exchange and towns.

These are broad historical patterns rather than sharp boundaries. Pastoralism, farming and craft production continued to coexist, and different regions experienced the changes at different times.

Prelims focus

  • Jana: A people or community; janapada: Territory associated with a settled jana.
  • The upper Ganga-Yamuna region was important in later Vedic settlement growth.
  • Painted Grey Ware is associated with several settlements in this region.
  • From around the 6th century BCE, mahajanapadas developed with fortified capitals and more regular resource collection.
  • Second urbanisation refers to later early historic urban growth, distinct from the earlier Harappan cities.
  • Trap: Iron technology contributed to change but was neither the only cause nor a uniform explanation for urban growth.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, 2018–19 edition, Chapter 6, 'Kingdoms, Kings and an Early Republic', printed pp. 54–60, and Chapter 9, 'Vital Villages, Thriving Towns', printed pp. 87–94; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 2, 'Kings, Farmers and Towns', sections 2.1 and 5.2, printed pp. 29–30 and 38–39; INFLIBNET e-PG Pathshala, Pre and Protohistoric Cultures of India, 'Technology in Ancient India', sections 1–3, and 'Iron Age – Society and Economy', sections 4–7 (consulted 17 November 2026).]

pictures.alt: A timeline from Harappan cities to early historic states, with continuous strands showing agriculture, pastoralism and crafts persisting across periods.
pictures.caption: The broad economic transition from early Vedic communities to early historic states.

title: Settlement Change: From Pastoral Villages to Janapadas and Early Towns
